name: The Libertines
label: Rough Trade
lede: Two songwriters who couldn't stand each other and couldn't do without each other made two albums for Rough Trade, broke up by way of a burglary, and somehow ended up running a hotel together in Margate.

hero.by: The Libertines at the HMV Forum, London, August 2010. Wikimedia Commons

eras.title: Plan A
eras.text: Pete Doherty and Carl Barât met through Doherty's sister, wrote songs in a run of shabby London flats and spent four years failing to get signed. Then the Strokes happened, and the Libertines' lawyer-turned-manager drew up a six-month plan to get them onto the same label.

years.h: Barât moves in with Doherty's sister, and meets Doherty
years.p: Barât was studying drama at Brunel and sharing a flat in Richmond with Amy-Jo Doherty. Lines from Shiver, released in 2024, date back to a Victorian garret on Upper Richmond Road West that year.

years.h: The Strand becomes the Libertines, after the Marquis de Sade
years.p: With their neighbor Scarborough Steve, Barât and Doherty take the new name from Sade's Lusts of the Libertines. "The Albions" was also on the list.
years.xp:
Both had dropped out by then: Barât after two years at Brunel, Doherty after one at Queen Mary. They took a flat on Camden Road and called it the Albion Rooms. Early gigs happened in the flat itself, and at Filthy MacNasty's in Islington, where Doherty pulled pints.

Barât had a line for their ambitions: "It's either to the top of the world, or the bottom of a canal."

years.h: Johnny Borrell plays bass for a spell
years.p: The future [[Razorlight|f2cb0435-d643-4fab-9587-fdb0279330a7]] frontman passes through alongside [[John Hassall|301fd0ff-c1d6-4e05-b35f-3964294dd806]], who joins on bass the following year.

years.h: A Warner Chappell lawyer, Banny Poostchi, takes the band on
years.p: She helps them record Legs XI, eight songs that later circulated as a fan bootleg. By December, still unsigned, drummer Paul Dufour, Hassall and Poostchi all walk away.

years.h: Rough Trade signs the Libertines four days before Christmas
years.p: The Strokes' success brought Poostchi back with a six-month "Plan A." A showcase for Rough Trade's James Endeacott on October 1 led to an audition for [[Geoff Travis|70437714-3183-4916-947f-e5ba2154d16a]] and Jeanette Lee on December 11.
years.xp:
Borrell skipped the October showcase. When they phoned him, he was on tour, as Wikipedia puts it, "living the high life." [[Gary Powell|254b6c7a-0112-4565-9642-359928f0f347]] came in on drums; Poostchi thought Dufour was "too old."

Hassall agreed to come back on bass on one condition set by the band: he'd stay in the background, because the Libertines were about Doherty and Barât.

eras.title: Up the bracket
eras.text: Signed and housed together in Bethnal Green, the Libertines played more than a hundred shows in a year, some of them in their own front room. Mick Jones of the Clash produced the album and mostly let them play.

years.h: 112a Teesdale Street becomes the Albion Rooms, and a venue
years.p: Doherty and Barât rent a flat in Bethnal Green and turn it into the base for their guerrilla gigs, announced at short notice to fans online.
years.xp: A 2003 film by Anne McCloy caught one of these gigs at the Albion Rooms being shut down by police after neighbors complained.

years.h: What a Waster is too sweary for daytime radio
years.p: The debut double A-side with I Get Along, produced by Bernard Butler, gets little airplay, a cleaned-up Radio 1 single of the week, and the band's first NME cover. It reaches number 37.

years.h: [[Mick Jones|01f8343c-06e2-4f05-a137-f8ea7efa85c4]] of the Clash produces Up the Bracket
years.p: Cut at RAK in St John's Wood, Jones's method was to let the band play a song through several times and pick the best take. The year's 100-plus gigs included support slots for the [[Sex Pistols|e5db18cb-4b1f-496d-a308-548b611090d3]] and [[Morrissey|013fa897-86db-41d3-8e9f-386c8a34f4e6]].

eras.title: From Wandsworth to the Tap'n'Tin
eras.text: Doherty's drug use and the people around it split the band's two songwriters. By summer he'd been left off a tour, broken into Barât's flat and gone to prison. By October Barât was waiting for him at the gate.

years.h: The Babyshambles Sessions, and two matching tattoos
years.p: In New York, Doherty and Barât get "Libertine" inked on their arms in Barât's handwriting. Barât then walks out of the sessions; Doherty finishes alone, and the tapes end up free online.

years.h: Doherty misses the train to Germany
years.p: After Barât skipped a birthday gig Doherty had set up for him, Doherty didn't show for the European tour. A guitar tech learned his parts; Barât then refused to have Doherty back until he got clean.

years.big: An antique guitar, a laptop, a mouth organ.
years.h: Doherty kicks in the door of Barât's flat while the band are in Japan
years.p: He took those and more from the basement flat. Doherty pleaded guilty to burglary and on September 8 was sentenced to six months, served in Wandsworth prison.
years.xp:
The Guardian described Doherty, then 24, as having had a £200-a-day heroin and crack habit for five years. His solicitor had asked for a community sentence so he could go into rehab.

On appeal the sentence was cut to two months. That summer the band played the Carling Weekend with Anthony Rossomando in Doherty's place.

yt: Don't Look Back into the Sun (official video)
years.h: Don't Look Back into the Sun reaches number 11
years.p: Their highest chart placing yet, with Butler back as producer and Doherty rarely in the room.

years.h: Barât meets Doherty at the prison gate. They play Chatham that night
years.p: Hassall and Powell turn up at the Tap'n'Tin in Chatham, Kent, though nobody expected them. NME named it Gig of the Year.

years.h: Three sold-out nights at the London Forum end in stage invasions
years.p: Q later put the run among its top 100 gigs of all time.

eras.title: Can't stand me now
eras.text: The second album was made with security guards between the two frontmen. It went to number one with Doherty already gone, and by December Barât had ended the band rather than carry on without him.

years.h: Three nights at Brixton Academy, and a new manager
years.p: Poostchi steps down and Creation Records founder [[Alan McGee|ffacc13a-01e5-4b5d-a455-6a7f302ac9ce]] takes over. The band also win Best Band at the NME Awards on the strength of one single.

years.h: Mick Jones tries again, with bodyguards in the studio
years.p: Sessions with Butler had collapsed. Back with Jones, security hired to protect the two frontmen also had to keep them from fighting. Doherty left before the mixing.

years.h: The last set together for six years, at Barât's club night
years.p: Fresh out of the Priory a second time, Doherty finds Barât at the Infinity Club and says he's going to a Thai monastery, Wat Tham Krabok, to get clean. They play a short set.
years.xp:
It was also the last time Doherty and Barât would speak for more than nine months. Barât's club night was called Dirty Pretty Things until a dispute forced a rename.

The band's public line: when Doherty cleaned up, he'd be "immediately welcomed back." By then his other band, Babyshambles, was taking off.

years.cap: The Libertines without Doherty at the Fillmore, San Francisco, October 2004
years.h: Can't Stand Me Now, a duet about the breakup, reaches number 2
years.p: Doherty and Barât trade lines about their own falling-out over a song they wrote together.

years.h: The Libertines goes to number one with Doherty already gone
years.p: Jones produced again. Roger Sargent's cover, Barât looking up as Doherty leans on his shoulder, became the band's defining image. NME voted it the second-best album of 2004.
play: What Became of the Likely Lads

years.big: Babyshambles on one side, Dirty Pretty Things on the other.
years.h: One last show in Paris, then Barât ends the Libertines
years.p: Still touring without Doherty, Barât decides he won't keep the name going without him.
years.xp:
Doherty already had Babyshambles. Barât formed Dirty Pretty Things, taking his old club night's name, with Powell on drums and Rossomando on guitar, and McGee as manager.

Barât later admitted how far the split took him: "There was one point where I very very nearly, just to be close to him, started taking full-on heroin."

eras.title: Two nights at Reading, then nothing
eras.text: Six years after Paris, all four came back for a summer. The reunion got the reviews the band had rarely been in one piece to collect, then everyone went back to their own projects.

years.h: A reunion press conference turns into a guerrilla gig
years.p: Two days after announcing Reading and Leeds, the band meet the press at the Boogaloo pub in Highgate and end up playing the old songs.

years.h: Back at the Forum, for fans only
years.p: A warm-up for 300 friends, family and press on August 24, then a sold-out fans-only night.

yt: The Libertines live at Reading Festival, 2010
years.h: Reading and Leeds, as special guests to [[Arcade Fire|52074ba6-e495-4ef3-9bb4-0703888a9f68]]
years.p: Doherty promised these sets would be remembered. Press and fans agreed, and by 2011 there were still no plans to do it again.

years.h: There Are No Innocent Bystanders premieres
years.p: Roger Sargent, the band's photographer since their first show, films the 2010 reunion. It premiered at the East End Film Festival and toured O2 Academies in 2012.

eras.title: Albion, by the sea
eras.text: A Hyde Park offer turned into a record deal, a third album finished in Thailand and, eventually, a hotel of their own in Margate. The fourth album was made there and went to number one twenty years after the second.

years.h: Headlining Hyde Park, with the Pogues on the undercard
years.p: From the stage they add three nights at Alexandra Palace in September. In November the band sign to Virgin EMI.

years.h: Doherty finishes rehab in Thailand and joins the recording
years.p: He'd been at the Hope Rehab Centre. Barât's photo from the sessions came captioned "Kitchen sink dramas over track listings."

years.h: Surprise guests on Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage
years.p: Ed Harcourt joined them.

years.h: Anthems for Doomed Youth, eleven years after the last album
years.p: Pushed back a week to meet demand for the launch shows, billed as Somewhere Over the Railings. An arena tour followed in January 2016 with [[Sleaford Mods|09d8290b-6ada-422f-8ce3-19349fb1c15d]] among the support acts.

years.cap: Doherty and Barât share a mic at Festival des Vieilles Charrues, Carhaix
years.h: Jeremy Corbyn opens their show at Prenton Park
years.p: The Labour leader gave a speech from the stage before the set, in the run-up to the general election.

years.h: The band open a hotel and studio in Margate: the Albion Rooms
years.p: They bought 31 Eastern Esplanade in Cliftonville in 2017, owned equally by all four. Barât called it their "HQ" and admitted it was "backbreaking work to make it break even."

years.cap: Barât and Doherty at Glastonbury, June 24, 2022
years.h: Early drummer Paul Dufour dies
years.p: Dufour played drums with the band in 2000, before Powell.

q: Everything I write is for Carl.
years.h: All Quiet on the Eastern Esplanade goes to number one
years.p: Written by Doherty and Barât in Jamaica in September 2022 and recorded in three weeks at the Albion Rooms. Their first UK number one since 2004.
years.xp:
"There's genuine love there," Barât told Guitar.com. "There's a version of myself that only exists with Pete."

Doherty told the Guardian the first thing he thinks after writing any song is what Barât will make of it.
play: All Quiet on the Eastern Esplanade

years.cap: The Libertines at the Lido, Margate
years.h: The hotel closes to guests; the Albion Rooms stays a studio
years.p: Barât said they wanted to "spend less time worrying about running a hospitality enterprise."

years.h: A sold-out UK tour, then Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage in 2025
years.p: Doherty, Barât, Hassall and Powell are still the lineup, with Andrew Newlove and Gary Hodgkiss added on tour since 2023.
